children.value: In propositional logic, we typically have a very simple mapping between propositions and logic variables: one variable per proposition. In first order logic, this is not so simple because of the variables and quantifiers. As we know, first order logic requires us to provide an interpretation, which means we cannot treat first order logic in the same abstract way that we treated propositional logic. In particular, we will need to:
Specify what values our variables can take.
Let’s consider a simple problem, express it in first order logic, and then write a Kanren program to solve it.

Anjali, Brian, and Chen graduated from QUB on different days this summer. One of them studied French, one studied Geography, one read History. One scored a good 60%, one acheived a very good 65%, and the other an excellent 70%.
We have acquired some knowledge about who studied what and what their marks were. However, our knowledge is incomplete. Here is what we know:
The person who studied French scored 65%.
Let’s express this in first order logic. We will define a predicate

We now have to write goals that embody our knowledge. How do we go about this?

Let’s now modify this to include another piece of information:

Anjali, Brian, and Chen graduated from QUB on different days this summer. One of them studied French, one studied Geography, one read History. One scored a good 60%, one acheived a very good 65%, and the other an excellent 70%. One of them graduated on the 2nd July, one graduated on the 3rd July, one graduated on the 4th July.
The person who studied French scored 65%.
Chen graduated on the day before Anjali.
Our existing goals are therefore modified to (for $d\in{2,3,4}):

children.value: We can now code these up. We will need to make some adjustments to the rules that we already have to accomodate the additional variable. We will also have to figure out how to deal with the new information that something happened “before” something else.
Finally, let us consider a variant of this problem where we have a negative constraint:
The person who studied French scored 65%.
Chen graduated on the day before Anjali.
Anjali did not graduate on the 4th.

children.value: Kanren does not provide us with a negation operation. There are sound technical reasons for this. Briefly, the “easy” way to implement this is so-called

. This is essentially the idea that if you can’t prove a statement to be true then it must be false. This works for propositional logic but is unable to resolve values of variables in first order logic. There are techniques available for

, but these are all super-exponential in time complexity. This means that some creativity is necessary. Here, we adopt the rather crude method of constructing a positive goal by excluding the desired negative goal. This method is not viable for very large problems.
